Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

If the basement NAS is offline during a scheduled import, keep the originals on the workstation and retry only after it reconnects; otherwise, import the originals to the NAS. If the old laptop is to be retired, make erasure a later step only after the export has been verified. Keep the request clear and practical.

REFERENCE NOTES
Mina and Kenji Morita live in a two-storey house in Eugene, Oregon, with their daughter, Aiko, who is in her final year of high school, and Kenji’s mother, Sachiko, who visits for several months each year. The family has been collecting digital pictures since 2008. Mina usually takes photographs on a Pixel phone, Kenji uses an iPhone, and Aiko has pictures on a school-issued camera that she is allowed to bring home but cannot install archive software on. Sachiko has a small Android phone with a limited amount of free storage. Kenji’s sister Naomi and Mina’s brother Luis live in other states and receive selected family albums. The household would like one archive that does not depend on any one phone staying in service.

The existing collection is split across a 2017 MacBook, two phones, an external USB drive labelled “MORITA OLD PHOTOS,” and a flatbed scanner. The MacBook contains folders by year, but several imported folders have names such as “New Folder 3” and “April copy.” The USB drive has scans of printed pictures from Mina’s parents’ albums, including handwritten dates on some of the scans’ filenames. A few folders contain edited copies beside the original camera files. The family has not yet compared the devices or drive to determine how many exact or near-duplicate files there are. Mina remembers that one folder called “Hana graduation” includes both the ceremony and a later dinner, while Kenji thinks the dinner pictures are in a separate folder.

Their home network has a small NAS in a ventilated cupboard in the basement, connected to the router by Ethernet. The NAS is powered down for occasional electrical work and has also been unavailable during two router replacements. The family schedules phone imports for Sunday evenings, but that timing is not guaranteed: Aiko’s camera is normally connected by cable, and Sachiko sometimes asks Mina to copy pictures while visiting. The MacBook remains the only computer with a card reader that works reliably. Kenji would prefer not to leave the NAS exposed to public internet access. He says, “I want the originals to stay ours even if we share a few albums.” The family has not chosen a cloud service or agreed to pay for one.

Sharing expectations differ by album. Mina and Kenji want Naomi and Luis to see pictures from the annual summer picnic and the grandparents’ anniversary, but the relatives should not be able to edit or delete the archive originals. Aiko sometimes makes an album for a school theatre production and may include classmates who are not relatives. Sachiko has asked that pictures from her 80th birthday be easy to view on her phone, including when she is travelling. Mina said, “Let’s not assume that a family event means every picture is ready to send around.” The family has not documented a consistent way to record permission from people who appear in photographs. Some older prints include people whose names nobody in the household can identify.

The collection also includes photographs that the family considers personal even when the people pictured are close relatives. Kenji has a small private album of pictures from a medical fundraiser, and Mina keeps scans of letters and family documents in a folder beside the old photographs. Those files should not become part of a shared album merely because they are stored near photographs from the same year. Aiko would like to keep some images from school productions off the household TV slideshow. No one has decided whether the family should use an album tag, a folder, or another method to distinguish private material. The relatives’ shared collection is intended for selected pictures, not as a complete mirror of the household archive.

The family has talked about keeping the NAS in the basement because it is out of the way, but they understand that a single device is not a complete recovery plan. The USB drive is currently stored in a desk drawer near the MacBook, and both are in the same upstairs room. During a winter leak in 2022, the basement cupboard stayed dry, but water reached part of the upstairs hallway; none of the photo equipment was damaged. Mina’s aunt lives about twenty minutes away and has offered to keep a sealed drive in her filing cabinet, though nobody has prepared one for her yet. The family wants recovery instructions that distinguish a copy stored elsewhere from a drive that remains beside the computer.

The old MacBook’s battery no longer holds a charge, and its operating system is too old for several current photo applications. It can still read the external drive and export folders to a newer computer when connected to power. Kenji has asked whether they can eventually stop relying on it, but Mina wants to be able to open representative older scans before it is wiped or donated. In March, Kenji copied a test folder to a borrowed laptop and found that the filenames were intact, but they did not check whether the exported files opened or whether the folder count matched. If the family retires the MacBook after a full export, they want that decision to follow checks of the copied files rather than precede them. Aiko has offered to help review recent phone pictures, but she cannot manage the archive settings on her school camera.

The household would like a retention setting that is understandable to all four family members and does not remove a file from the only place it exists. They have not agreed that every import should be kept forever, and no one has specified a retention period beyond the value in the configuration excerpt below. Mina prefers keeping an untouched original when edits are made, while Kenji wants edited versions to remain easy to find beside the corresponding original. They would also like the setup to make clear which locations are local, which are shared with relatives, and what happens when a device is unavailable. The family is willing to follow a short monthly check, but they have not assigned that task to a particular person.

Configuration excerpt supplied by the family:
[local_archive]
retain_days = 18
allow_remote = false
name = "local-copy"

The family has not tested this excerpt with the NAS software, and they do not know whether it represents the complete configuration or a single section. It is included as the exact local-archive setting they have on hand. The technician should be able to distinguish that supplied setting from the unresolved choices in the notes, and the family wants the plan to account for the NAS being temporarily unavailable during an import. Their main concern is a usable, understandable archive for ordinary family use, not a public gallery or a one-time cleanup of every historical folder.
